_note: Monte Carlo scenario inputs (spec §5b; model revised 2026-11-16, DECISIONS #23). Each input is a central value plus a spread: every simulated future draws the input from a symmetric triangular distribution centre ± spread, clipped to [min, max]. status: from_layer2 = calibrated from CBP statistics; from_layer3 = Sayari; sourced_estimate = a central value we set from the cited sources; placeholder = structural default awaiting a source, shown with a badge on the page. Every value can be changed on the page.

thresholds.label: Blacklisted companies only
thresholds.plain: only when the supplier itself is on the US blacklist (the UFLPA Entity List)

thresholds.label: Companies customs has acted against (today)
thresholds.plain: from the company groups it has already publicly detained or refused solar shipments from, which is what the enforcement record shows today

thresholds.label: 2–3 steps back
thresholds.plain: when a blacklisted or Xinjiang company appears 2–3 steps back in the supply chain

thresholds.label: Up to 4 steps back
thresholds.plain: up to 4 steps back, where the link is to a solar-relevant input

thresholds.label: + companies sharing an owner
thresholds.plain: up to 4 steps back, and also when a supplier shares an owner with a blacklisted company

thresholds.label: + companies named by researchers
thresholds.plain: everywhere the data can see: up to 4 steps back, shared owners, and companies named in independent research (ASPI, Sheffield Hallam)

step_increments_placeholder._note: Fallback only, used if Layer 3 is missing: flagged share of US supply at each step (triangular low/mode/high, cumulative). Not data.

inputs.label: How many flagged shipments customs stops
inputs.question: Of the shipments the rule flags, what share does US customs actually stop and inspect?
inputs.source: Not calibratable yet: at today's reach Sayari flags no shipments, so there is no flagged base to divide CBP detentions by (pipeline/notes/layer3_validation.md).

inputs.label: How many stopped shipments are released
inputs.question: Of the shipments customs stops, what share is released after the importer submits supply chain paperwork?
inputs.source: Replaced by CBP released ÷ (released + denied) when Layer 2 statistics are present.

inputs.label: How much blocked supply gets back in
inputs.question: Of the supply that is blocked for good, what share finds another way into the US (rerouted through other countries or suppliers)?
inputs.source: Estimate from sources: after the 2023 circumvention finding and 2024–25 duties, a quarter to a half of lost volume reappeared from other countries within quarters (SI-008, SI-009). UFLPA blocks are company- not country-based, so the centre is set lower (0.3).

inputs.label: How long stopped shipments are held
inputs.question: While customs reviews the paperwork, how many months does a stopped shipment sit at the border (whether it's released or not)?
inputs.source: Estimate from sources: CBP says a complete document package takes two to three weeks (SI-010); pending solar cases averaged about two months, with contested cases running many months (SI-011). 2 months (0.5–3.5).

inputs.label: How exposed the untraced supply is
inputs.question: About 9% of supply can't be traced. Compared with the supply we can trace, how likely is it to carry the same links?
inputs.source: Assumption: untraced supply is about as exposed as traced supply at the same reach, give or take half. Linked to rerouting (ρ = 0.5): opaque supply chains are also the leakiest.

inputs.label: Solar stock already in the US
inputs.question: How many months of normal US demand for panels is already sitting in US warehouses or in transit?
inputs.source: Estimate from sources: US module inventory was ~11 months of demand at end-2023 (SI-003), ~5.6 months by April 2025 (SI-004) and 'depleting rapidly' (SI-005). No 2026 figure is published, so 4 months (1.5–6.5) is our estimate.

inputs.label: Time before new suppliers deliver
inputs.question: How many months before replacement suppliers start shipping?
inputs.source: Estimate from sources: no published figure for qualifying a new module supplier. Bankability needs projects over two years (SI-012); new factories take 1–3 years (SI-013). 9 months (5–13) assumes existing non-linked makers scale up.

inputs.label: How fast new suppliers fill the gap
inputs.question: Once they start, how much of normal US demand can replacement suppliers add each month?
inputs.source: Estimate from sources: US module capacity grew ~23–28 GW a year in 2024–25 (SI-006), about 4–5% of annual demand per month in nameplate terms, but first-year output ran at 20–45% of capacity (SI-007) and growth stalled in 2026. Cells, needed for traceable silicon modules, add less. 1.5% (0.3–2.7%).

presets.label: Today’s enforcement
presets.blurb: Customs acts on the companies it has stopped before.

presets.label: Look further back
presets.blurb: Customs checks 2–3 steps up the supply chain.

presets.label: Look everywhere
presets.blurb: Every link the data can see counts.

presets.label: Everywhere, and strict
presets.blurb: Every link counts, and customs rarely accepts the paperwork.

model: Flagged = share of US cell + module shipments from suppliers the rule would flag at this reach (Sayari), plus the untraced share × (flagged ÷ traced) × the untraced-exposure multiplier.
Lost = Kept out × (1 − share that gets back in another way).
Serious disruption = Lost is above the line you set (default 20% of US supply).

Shortage months = the longer of (a) supply lost for good: max(0, delay before new suppliers + Lost ÷ monthly replacement − stock in months × 100 ÷ Lost), and (b) supply held at the border: max(0, months held − stock in months × 100 ÷ Stopped). Stock runs down first; any time left over is a shortage.
